title: PR #157 review feedback for asset representation attach
description: Close the gaps a review of PR #157 found between the branch and the acceptance criteria of issue #143 and its parent #140.

stories.title: Return 422 naming the observations that block a tax calculation
stories.description: A calculation blocked by unresolved provider observations currently surfaces as HTTP 500 and says nothing about what is unresolved. Return the declared 422 and name the blocking observations so a user can act on them.
acceptance_criteria: Requesting a tax calculation for a source with at least one unresolved provider observation responds with HTTP 422, not 500.
The 422 body identifies each blocking provider observation by provider and currency code, so a client can show what is unresolved without guessing from missing IDs.
The tax calculation service returns the blocking observations, not only a count.
A source with no unresolved observation still calculates normally and responds 200.
The gate stays source-wide and all-years: an unresolved observation blocks every requested year, because FIFO inventory carries across year boundaries.
implementation_notes: The error type already declares its HTTP status; the REST error mapping is what falls through to the internal-server-error branch.
Keep the blocking observation list bounded so one source with a large unresolved long tail cannot produce an unbounded response body.

Parent issue #140 user story 22 requires unresolved states to be represented explicitly rather than inferred from missing IDs or zero values, and user story 5 requires the user to see which observations make the calculation incomplete.
testing_notes: Add a rest-api integration test that seeds a source with an unresolved observation and asserts the 422 status and the named observations. It must fail before the change.
Add a persistence test asserting the service reports the blocking observations for the source.

stories.title: Give resolution jobs attempt limits and lease identity
stories.description: The resolution job table has status and timestamps but no attempt count, lease, or error message, so a crashed worker strands a job in processing and a permanently failing job retries forever. Add the hardening the queue needs before anything dispatches these jobs.
acceptance_criteria: A resolution job records attempt count, attempt limit, start time, heartbeat, next retry time, owning worker, and last error.
Claiming a job increments its attempt count and records the claiming worker and start time.
A job released after a failure becomes runnable again only once its next retry time has passed, and the delay grows with the attempt count.
A job that reaches its attempt limit becomes failed and is never handed out again.
A job left in processing by a worker that stopped heartbeating can be reclaimed by another worker.
Two workers claiming the same job concurrently result in exactly one claim; the other sees the job as not claimable.
The schema change ships as a generated migration.
implementation_notes: Mirror the columns and checks already proven on the source-sync job table rather than inventing a second vocabulary: attempt count, attempt limit, queued/started/heartbeat/completed timestamps, next retry time, worker id, and error message.
The repository contract owns claim, heartbeat, release, and fail. Keep table details out of the sync orchestration layer.
The product is pre-launch, so prefer a clean schema over a compatibility bridge.
testing_notes: Add integration tests for the retry-with-backoff path, the attempt-limit exhaustion path, stale-lease reclaim, and concurrent claim. Each must fail before the change.
Assert observable job state through the repository contract rather than by reading columns directly where a contract method already exposes it.

stories.title: Dispatch pending resolution jobs from the worker
stories.description: Nothing runs the resolution job executor outside of tests, so scheduled jobs stay pending forever and no observation is ever resolved. Give the worker a queue and dispatcher for them.
acceptance_criteria: The worker process runs a resolution consumer alongside the existing source-sync consumer, on its own queue.
A job scheduled by sync is picked up and executed without any manual trigger, and reaches a terminal state.
Enqueueing the same job twice results in one execution; the second sees the job as already claimed and does no work.
A job whose evidence revision no longer matches its observation completes as stale without calling any external service.
A failing execution releases the job for retry through the attempt and backoff rules rather than looping immediately.
Dispatch failures are logged with structured data and do not crash the worker.
implementation_notes: Mirror the shape of the existing source-sync consumer layer in the worker app, including its pending-dispatch poller, worker identity, and lock duration, so operators have one mental model for both queues.
Keep the executor itself unchanged in shape: the consumer claims and dispatches, the executor decides.
Wire the executor's dependencies in the worker composition root the same way the source-sync executor is wired.
Parent issue #140 user story 27 requires external registry calls to stay off the sync critical path, so the consumer must be independent of source sync.
testing_notes: Test the processor through the existing worker test seam rather than against a real Redis.
Cover: a pending job is dispatched and executed, a duplicate dispatch is a no-op, and an execution failure releases the job for retry.
An end-to-end test that a scheduled job reaches a terminal state without a manual executor call is the criterion that proves the original gap is closed.

stories.title: Retry transient CoinGecko failures instead of failing closed
stories.description: Every non-2xx status and transport error becomes the same upstream failure, which the executor records as a permanent fail-closed decision that is never revisited at the same evidence revision. A rate limit must not become a durable wrong answer.
acceptance_criteria: A rate-limited, server-error, timed-out, or unreachable CoinGecko response releases the job for retry and records no durable decision.
A not-found response and an undecodable payload still fail closed with a durable decision, because retrying cannot change them.
The client retries a transient failure a bounded number of times with backoff before giving up on the attempt.
The request has a timeout, so a hanging upstream cannot hold a job lease open indefinitely.
The coin identifier is URL-encoded into the request path.
After a transient failure is retried and then succeeds, the observation reaches the same decision it would have reached on a first-attempt success.
implementation_notes: The evidence client contract needs to distinguish retryable from terminal so the executor can act on it; today both collapse into one upstream-failure value.
Retry belongs at the fetch boundary and job release belongs at the executor boundary. Keep the decision policy itself unaware of transport concerns.
Read the retry and timeout settings through Effect Config rather than hardcoding, and follow the existing package convention for configuration.
The public CoinGecko API allows roughly ten to thirty requests per minute, so rate limiting is expected traffic, not an exceptional condition.
testing_notes: Drive the client through a controlled HTTP stub covering 429, 500, timeout, transport error, 404, and an undecodable 200.

Add an executor-level test proving a retryable failure leaves no decision row and leaves the job runnable, and that a terminal failure records fail-closed exactly once. It must fail before the change.

stories.title: Make resolution decision history append-only
stories.description: The decisions table allows exactly one row per observation and evidence revision and swallows conflicting inserts, so it is a single-row projection labelled as history. Reshape it so a superseding decision can be appended and linked to the one it replaces.
acceptance_criteria: A decision can be superseded by appending a new decision that links to the decision it replaces; the replaced decision is preserved unchanged.
Exactly one decision is active per provider observation and evidence revision at any time; the database rejects a second active one.
Reading the current decision for an observation returns the active decision, and reading its history returns every decision in order.
Re-running a job at the same evidence revision does not create a second decision and does not rewrite the existing one; the caller can tell that nothing new was recorded.
The executor acts on that signal instead of ignoring it: a replay is logged and does not silently repeat its side effects as if it were a first decision.
The schema change ships as a generated migration.
implementation_notes: Drop the unique constraint on observation and evidence revision, add a link from a decision to the decision it supersedes, and enforce a single active decision with a partial unique index.
Superseding is #148's feature. This story only makes the schema and repository able to hold an appended supersession; do not build the human approval flow.
Parent issue #140 user story 44 requires superseding decisions to be appended rather than old decisions edited.
The product is pre-launch, so a hard migration is acceptable and preferred over a compatibility bridge.
testing_notes: Add integration tests for appending a supersession, for rejecting a second active decision, and for reading current versus full history.
Add a test that a second execution at the same evidence revision reports that nothing was recorded and leaves the original decision intact. It must fail before the change.

stories.title: Store evidence snapshots as authority-scoped records
stories.description: Evidence lives in two hardcoded columns named after today's two authorities, and it does not record where the evidence came from or when it was retrieved. Move it to authority-scoped records so a new authority is a new row rather than a new column.
acceptance_criteria: Each decision stores zero or more evidence records, one per authority and claim kind.
An evidence record captures the authority, the claim kind, where the evidence came from, when it was retrieved, the decoded claim, the raw payload, and the evidence revision it was gathered at.
The same authority and claim kind cannot be recorded twice for one decision.
Reading a decision returns its evidence records, and an attach decision reproduces the exact chain and registry evidence it was made from.
The two hardcoded evidence columns are gone.
The schema change ships as a generated migration.
implementation_notes: Parent issue #140 user story 37 requires every automatic decision tied to immutable evidence and a policy revision so it can be reproduced.
Issues #145 and #146 each add another authority, so the shape must accept a new authority without a schema change.
Keep the raw payload separable from the decoded claim: the decoded claim is what the policy read, the raw payload is what the authority actually returned.
Do not widen trust: recording an authority's evidence says nothing about which claims it is allowed to prove.
testing_notes: Cover: an attach decision records both chain and registry evidence, a fail-closed decision records the evidence it had, and a duplicate authority and claim kind for one decision is rejected.
Prove a stored decision can be reproduced from its evidence records without reading any provider payload table.

stories.title: Audit representation ownership independently of the observing provider
stories.description: Every ownership conclusion is keyed on the provider observation that happened to trigger it, so a second provider observing the same representation starts from nothing. Record which economic asset owns a representation as its own fact.
acceptance_criteria: Ownership of a network representation by an economic asset is recorded keyed on the representation identity, not on the provider observation that triggered it.
A second provider observing the same representation reuses the settled owner and does not need to re-derive it from registry evidence.
A decision claiming a different owner for an already-owned representation is rejected by the database, not only by the policy.
A resolution decision references the representation it attached through a foreign key, so a deleted representation cannot leave a dangling reference.
The provider mapping decision and the representation ownership decision are separately readable, matching the two decisions the design already names.
The schema change ships as a generated migration.
implementation_notes: Parent issue #140 user story 38 requires the representation-to-economic-asset relationship to be audited directly so a future provider can reuse the conclusion without inheriting one provider's history.
The representation identity is the chain plus the contract or mint address, or the chain alone for a native representation. Canonicalize it the same way the resolution policy does.
Do not build the second provider integration itself; #145 owns that. Prove reuse through an existing provider path or a controlled fixture.
The product is pre-launch, so a hard migration is acceptable.
testing_notes: Add a persistence-level test that a conflicting ownership claim is rejected by the database. This gap is named in issue #143's own testing plan.
Add a test that a second observation of the same representation resolves to the already-settled owner without new registry evidence.
Each test must fail before the change.

stories.title: Canonicalize chain facts once and report the real pending reason
stories.description: The executor and the policy canonicalize addresses differently, so two distinct case-sensitive addresses can collapse into one exact fact, and two different pending situations report the same reason. Both hide information the audit trail is supposed to preserve.
acceptance_criteria: Two observations whose addresses differ only in case on a chain where case is significant are treated as conflicting facts and fail closed, rather than collapsing into one fact.
Two observations of the same address on a chain where case is not significant still collapse into one fact.
An observation with no candidate economic asset and an observation with several candidates stay pending but record different reasons, so the audit trail says which situation occurred.
Two malformed non-native representations with no address do not produce the same representation identity.
Looking up an owned representation for a fact with no address fails closed instead of querying for an empty address.
The unreachable branch in the representation type compatibility check is gone, and the check's behavior is unchanged.
implementation_notes: There must be exactly one address canonicalizer, owned by the resolution policy in core, and the executor must use it.
Widening candidate discovery beyond symbol match is #144's job. This story only fixes the reason code, not the search.
Parent issue #140 user story 31 requires exact chain identity to come from chain evidence, with names and symbols staying display data.
testing_notes: These are all unit-level policy and executor behaviors; prefer unit tests over integration tests.
Each criterion needs a test that fails before the change. The case-collapse test is the important one: today the wrong answer is silently the last observation seen.

stories.title: Schedule a job for every unresolved observation and never lose one to a rollback
stories.description: The catalog path filters to observations that already have a pending-review mapping, so a brand new observation with no mapping row is never scheduled. A second path schedules a job and then fails, which can roll the job back inside an outer transaction.
acceptance_criteria: A newly discovered provider observation with no mapping row is scheduled for resolution, whichever path discovered it.
An observation with an approved mapping is not scheduled.
Scheduling stays idempotent per observation and evidence revision across both discovery paths.
A scheduled job survives the failure that follows it: after the reference-mapping path reports an unmapped asset, the job is still present and runnable.
The transfer amount conversion that was already a string is no longer wrapped in a redundant conversion.
The leg derivation parameter that now receives every canonical transfer is named for what it actually receives.
implementation_notes: The two discovery paths currently disagree on which mapping states count as unresolved. Settle on one rule and apply it in both.

The schedule-then-fail behavior needs an experiment, not a reading: prove whether an outer transaction rolls the scheduled job back before deciding how to fix it. If it does, the job must be committed independently of the failure.
Parent issue #140 user story 28 requires one resolution job per distinct observation and evidence revision so many users seeing the same asset do not duplicate research.
testing_notes: Add an integration test that discovers a brand new observation through the catalog path and asserts a job exists. It must fail before the change.
Add a test that runs the reference-mapping path inside an outer transaction that then fails, and asserts the job is still there.

stories.title: Close the remaining coverage gaps from the issue's own testing plan
stories.description: Issue #143 names contract, concurrency, and replay tests that the branch does not have. Fill in what earlier stories did not already cover, and turn the attach test's implied no-refetch claim into an asserted one.
acceptance_criteria: The attach replay test asserts the provider was fetched exactly once, instead of only counting fetches without checking the count.
There is a test for each policy outcome reaching durable storage: attach, pending, and fail-closed.
There is a concurrency test for two workers racing for one job, and a test that a duplicate dispatch is a no-op.
There is a test that a released job is picked up again and completes on a later attempt.
Rematerialization is proven to run from stored raw records with no provider call.
No test asserts on internal call order where an observable outcome would do.
implementation_notes: This story adds tests only. If a test cannot be written without a production change, that change belongs to the story that owns the behavior.
Skip anything an earlier story already covered rather than duplicating it.
Follow the existing integration test kit rather than building new harness code.
testing_notes: Every added test must be meaningful on its own: a test that passes before and after the whole batch is not closing a gap.
Prefer asserting observable state through repository contracts over reading tables directly.
